title: When the Witness Sings
premise: Xanthe Okonkwo, archivist of St. Aldhelm's Cathedral, catalogues the belongings of the late Dean Ambrose Vellacott when a letter arrives postmarked one day after the dean's funeral — a confession to a murder committed thirty years ago, sealed inside the crypt no one can open. Following the letter's clues through the cathedral's records, Xanthe discovers the 'accidental' death of a young chorister in 1994 was murder, and that the witnesses who covered it up now hold the city's most powerful offices. As Xanthe closes in, the conspirators move to seal the crypt — and Xanthe — forever, forcing a final reckoning in the crypt itself where the truth is sung aloud by the last living witness. Justice comes not from the law, which the powerful already own, but from exposure: the confession is broadcast during the cathedral's Christmas service, and the guilty are undone in public.
about_author: Coral Coldharbour spent a decade cataloguing parish records in coastal England before turning to crime fiction, and her novels are known for their reverence for archives and their suspicion of institutions. She writes in a converted vestry on the North Norfolk coast, where the tide keeps its own schedule of secrets.

chapters.title: The Day After
chapters.summary: Xanthe Okonkwo's POV. While cataloguing the late Dean Vellacott's papers, Xanthe receives a confession letter postmarked the day after the funeral, confessing to a murder and pointing to the sealed crypt. The emotional beat is unease: grief for the dean colliding with the impossibility of a letter that should not exist.

chapters.title: What the Dean Kept
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Searching the dean's private office, Xanthe finds a hidden key and a 1994 inquest file on chorister Toby Merriweather, ruled accidental drowning. The beat is dawning dread as the confession's details match the file exactly — details never made public.

chapters.title: The Locked Crypt
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe attempts the crypt door and finds the lock changed — recently, and without the chapter's knowledge. Verger Edith Sloane warns him to let the dead rest. The beat is isolation: the first hint that someone alive is actively protecting the secret.

chapters.title: Choristers' Row
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe tracks down former choristers from 1994, finding them scattered, frightened, or dead — two 'accidents' in five years. One, Marcus Pell, agrees to talk then cancels. The beat is mounting alarm as the pattern of silencing emerges.

chapters.title: The Benefactor
chapters.summary: Marcus Pell's POV. Pell, now a wealthy developer, recalls the night Toby died and the men who decided the story: a young policeman, a rising councillor, and the then-succentor. He burns his old photographs. The beat is guilt curdling into fear as he realizes someone is collecting the witnesses.

chapters.title: Postmark
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe investigates the confession letter itself: the paper is old cathedral stock, the handwriting the dean's — yet postmarked after his death. Either the dean arranged a dead man's post, or someone forged it. The beat is intellectual vertigo: the evidence itself is a riddle.

chapters.title: The Succentor's Son
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe learns the succentor from 1994 is the father of the current chief constable, Rowan Vellacott — the dean's nephew. The family tree tightens into a noose. The beat is betrayal: the dean's own kin may be the killer he died protecting, or exposing.

chapters.title: Edith's Silence
chapters.summary: Edith Sloane's POV. The verger remembers the night in 1994 — she saw the boys return from the crypt, one soaked, one weeping — and was paid to forget. She nearly tells Xanthe, then finds her cottage searched. The beat is terror: the past has come for the small people first.

chapters.title: A Death in the Close
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Marcus Pell is found drowned in the close fountain, ruled a fall. Xanthe recognizes the staging — the same 'accident' as Toby's. The beat is fury and resolve: this is no longer a cold case but an active hunt, and Xanthe is on the list.

chapters.title: The Bishop's Bargain
chapters.summary: Bishop Anselm Cray's POV. The bishop, complicit in a 1994 cover-up that saved the cathedral's endowment, confronts Xanthe with an offer: silence, a promotion, and the crypt stays sealed. Xanthe refuses. The beat is temptation met with defiance, and the bishop's mask slipping.

chapters.title: What Toby Sang
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. In the music library, Xanthe finds Toby Merriweather's annotated scores — including a setting of a psalm whose marginal notes encode what he witnessed: the succentor's assault, the fight, the fall. The beat is heartbreak: the victim testified all along, in the only voice he had.

chapters.title: The Chief Constable
chapters.summary: Rowan Vellacott's POV. Rowan, who as a boy saw his father kill Toby and was made complicit, has spent thirty years burying it — including, Xanthe realizes, possibly the dean. Torn between loyalty and loathing, he destroys evidence while keeping one piece back. The beat is self-loathing and a crack of conscience.

chapters.title: Sealed Orders
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe is suspended from the archive on fabricated grounds and the crypt is scheduled for structural 'renovation' — permanent entombment of the evidence. Xanthe copies Toby's scores and goes underground into the city records. The beat is defiance under pressure.

chapters.title: The Undercroft
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. In the diocesan records office, Xanthe finds the dean's own investigation, begun a year before his death: names, payments, a copy of the original confession. The dean was killed, Xanthe believes, for exactly what Xanthe now holds. The beat is grim kinship with the dead man.

chapters.title: Night Visitors
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe's flat is ransacked; the copied scores are taken — but Xanthe has hidden the true pages in the organ loft. A warning note arrives: 'The crypt keeps what it keeps.' The beat is fear transmuted into cunning: they took decoys.

chapters.title: The Organist's Testimony
chapters.summary: Organist Fenella Marsh's POV. Fenella, Toby's friend in 1994, has kept silent for thirty years out of fear. Xanthe plays her Toby's psalm; she finishes the harmony he never completed and agrees to sing it publicly. The beat is grief becoming courage — the witness choosing to sing.

chapters.title: Christmas Eve
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. The conspirators gather for the cathedral's candlelit service, planning to seal the crypt at midnight. Xanthe, Edith, and Fenella make their own preparations. The beat is coiled anticipation: two plans set in motion in the same sacred building.

chapters.title: The Crypt Opens
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, climax part one. During the service, Xanthe descends with the dean's key and opens the crypt, finding Toby's effects and the succentor's written admission — and is trapped inside by the conspirators, who intend the 'renovation' to begin early. The beat is claustrophobic terror.

chapters.title: The Witness Sings
chapters.summary: Fenella's POV, climax part two. As the conspirators seal the door, Fenella begins Toby's psalm at the organ, Edith testifies from the pulpit, and the congregation — including journalists and Rowan, who finally turns — stops the sealing. The beat is catharsis: truth sung louder than power.

chapters.title: Reckoning
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The bishop resigns, the chief constable's father is arrested, and Rowan submits his own resignation and testimony. Xanthe, freed from the crypt, watches the law finally move — late, imperfect, but moving. The beat is exhausted, hard-won justice.

chapters.title: Toby's Stone
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A new memorial stone for Toby Merriweather is laid; the crypt is opened as a place of remembrance, not secrecy. Xanthe catalogs his short life with the care once denied him. The beat is mourning at last allowed.

chapters.title: The Empty Postmark
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, epilogue. A final letter arrives, unsigned: the dean's own hand, written before his death, mailed by an ally he trusted — revealing the dean chose Xanthe deliberately. Xanthe files it in the archive, the record complete. The beat is belonging: Xanthe is no longer just the keeper of the dead, but of the truth.
